paper_value: In contrast to the DMN, regions within the DAN —which closely overlapped with the younger > older activation clusters identified in our analysis (see Figure 5B and Supplemental Figure S4)—exhibited a distinct behavioral association in the older group. Specifically, under the highest task demand condition (MS–4L contrast), we observed a significant negative correlation between DAN activation and performance among older adults (see Figure 5C). That is, higher activation in canonical DAN regions such as the intraparietal sulcus and frontal eye fields was associated with poorer behavioral outcomes in the older cohort.

The authors report that younger adults displayed robust DMN deactivation during task engagement, which was associated with more efficient performance (lower IES), implying a negative association between DMN activity levels and task efficiency (formal coefficients are referenced in supplemental figures but not numerically detailed in the main text).
paper_value: Crucially, older adults also exhibited significant differences in task-induced DMN deactivation relative to younger adults. Specifically, older adults showed significantly less deactivation—or even positive activation—in canonical DMN regions, including the medial PFC and posterior cingulate cortex (p < .001; see Figure 5A and Supplemental Table S3). Younger adults, in contrast, displayed robust DMN deactivation during task engagement, which was associated with more efficient performance.
